name: Thiin
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Austin, Peter K. 1988/2015 Mantharta-language materials (extinct Thiin; sketch-level coverage plausibly includes stress)

sources.citation: Austin, Peter K. [2015-]. 'Spelling'. Jiwarli blog (jiwarli.com). (Jiwarli, djiw1241 — sister variety; Austin 2015 says Jiwarli and Thiin may be dialects of one language)
sources.note: 'All words in Jiwarli must end in a vowel, and all words begin with one and only one consonant. In general, stress (emphasis) falls on the first vowel of a word. So, for example, we have the word mandharda "person" which is pronounced as man-dha-rda with stress on the first syllable man. Do not put emphasis on later syllables as this sounds very unnatural in Jiwarli.' Applies to Jiwarli only; Thiin not named.

sources.citation: Klokeid, Terry J. 1969. Thargari phonology and morphology. Pacific Linguistics B-12. Canberra: ANU. (Tharrkari, dhar1247 — a sister Mantharta variety, not Thiin; Thiin is not mentioned)
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: Harvard print copy (Scan & Deliver or loan): WID Offsite Storage Philol 69.57.3 no.12 (also: archive.org controlled lending; hathitrust digitized, search-only (in copyright))
sources.note: §1.2.6, p. 5: 'All junctures share two characteristics: there is a potential for silence, and the first vowel following any juncture is more strongly stressed than others, in relatively slow speech. In the most rapidly spoken utterances observed, the stress differences were leveled, along with the disappearance of all pauses between words.' — i.e. word-initial stress for Tharrkari, used to define the phonological word.
Thiin (iin), Djiwarli (dze) and Dhargari (dhr) appear only in the ISO language list; no stress record for any of them.

sources.citation: Austin, Peter K. 2015. A Reference Grammar of the Mantharta Languages, Western Australia. Draft version 3.7, 15 July 2015. MS, SOAS, University of London. 106 pp. (Glottolog ref 474522; the only descriptive source Glottolog lists for Thiin)
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: open copy online (also: harvard online access (harvardkey))
sources.note: Nothing. Chapter 2 (pp. 37-46: 2.1 Consonant phonemes, 2.2 Minimal pairs 'To be written', 2.3 Phonotactics, 2.4 Tharrkari phonology, 2.5 Tharrkari morphophonemics, 2.6 loans) has no stress/accent subsection, and the words 'stress', 'accent', 'prominence' occur nowhere in the 106-page text. It states (p. 37) that Jiwarli, Warriyangka and Thiin are structurally similar and treated together for phonology, that Thiin data are 'the briefest of notes from a single session with Donald Eagles' plus O'Grady's Thiin vocabulary, and that Jiwarli is closer to Thiin than to the others.
Consonant/vowel tables only, no stress statement; they cite Austin 2015 (academia.edu), Klokeid 1969, Austin 1992 Warriyangga dictionary, Thieberger 1993.
